findings.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
findings.why: The replacement hint says "Canon III covers duties you take on only by accepting an engagement; Canon II covers how you conduct yourself whether or not anyone has hired you." This item is explicitly pre-acceptance: you tell them "up front" that the engagement is beyond you, i.e. you have not taken the engagement on. Applying the new test literally routes a well-prepared candidate to Canon II (truthfulness / staying within your competence, which the ISC2 Canon II objectives also cover verbatim), while the intended key is Canon III ("render only those services for which you are fully competent and qualified"). The bucket balance (2/2/2/2) confirms III is intended. Change 2 therefore fixed the counterparty misfire on one item and created a sharper one here: the hint now argues against the key.
findings.suggested_fix: Either re-key nothing and rewrite the item so the engagement already exists — e.g. "Midway through a client engagement you tell them a specialised cloud component is beyond what you are qualified to deliver, and you hand it to a specialist" — or reword hint 2 to "Canon III covers what you owe someone who is relying on you as their principal, including telling them what you cannot do; Canon II covers conduct owed to everyone." Do not leave "up front" in place with the current hint.

findings.item: You refuse to scan a network you have no written authorisation to test
findings.defect: two-home (Canon I vs Canon II), hints pull opposite ways
findings.why: The replacement item is legally framed (unauthorised scanning = illegality → Canon II, which the prompt gloss cues with "your own honesty and legality"), but hint 1 still asks "who is primarily being protected" — and the party protected by not scanning is the un-consulted network owner and the infrastructure, which reads as Canon I. ISC2 Canon I objectives also include "discourage unsafe practice". Hint 2 (engagement vs general conduct) supports II; hint 1 supports I. The item is defensible but the two hints now disagree on it, so the replacement did not land clean.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the legality the operative fact rather than the protected party: "You decline a request to port-scan a network because you have no written authorisation and doing so would be unlawful." Or drop "who is primarily being protected" from hint 1 (see next finding), which is what removes the Canon I pull.

findings.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
findings.defect: misleading-hint — the counterparty test was only removed from hint 2, not hint 1
findings.why: Change 2 claims the ethics hint no longer uses a counterparty test, but hint 1 is still exactly that: "Ask who is primarily being protected: the public, your own integrity, the client who hired you, or the profession itself." On this item the party being protected is a prospect — someone who has not hired you — which matches none of the four options cleanly and sits nearest "the client", steering candidates to Canon III. FUD selling also plausibly reads as Canon IV (it degrades the standing of the profession). Intended answer is Canon II ("give prudent advice; avoid raising unnecessary alarm"). So the removal was applied to one hint only and the residual test still misfires.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace hint 1 with a subject-matter test rather than a beneficiary test: "Ask what the situation is about: the safety of systems the public depends on (I), the legality and truthfulness of your own conduct (II), obligations to someone relying on you (III), or the credibility of the certification and the field (IV)."

findings.defect: misleading-hint — hint 1 describes availability loss but positions it as confidentiality
findings.why: Hint 1 reads "Ask what the victim actually lost: the ability to read it, trust in it, or access to it", and the three clauses map positionally onto the bucket order Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability. But a confidentiality breach is not the victim losing the ability to read data — it is a third party gaining it. Read literally, "lost the ability to read it" describes exactly what ransomware does, so a candidate who trusts hint 1 sorts this item into Confidentiality. Hint 2 rescues this one item by naming encryption explicitly; the framing error still stands for "Customer database exfiltrated and posted online" and "Attacker reads unencrypted traffic on public Wi-Fi", where the victim loses none of the three things listed.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite hint 1 from the attacker side: "Ask what the attacker gained or destroyed: the ability to see data they should not (C), the ability to change it undetected (I), or the ability to stop anyone reaching it (A)."

findings.item: Every system must have a named owner who is accountable for its security
findings.defect: two-home (Policy vs Standard) introduced by the replacement item
findings.why: The replacement removes the duplicate Policy wording, but hint 1 tells candidates to ask "is it mandatory, and does it name specific technology or specific steps?" This item is mandatory ("must") and states a specific, checkable requirement (one named accountable owner per system), so a candidate running the hint mechanically lands on Standard — the same reasoning that correctly yields Standard for "All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image". The intended answer is Policy (org-wide statement of intent, no technology named), and the sibling Policy item is the softer "The organisation will protect...", so the two Policy items are no longer duplicates but they no longer look like the same layer either.
findings.suggested_fix: Either soften it to a clear intent statement — "The organisation holds a named individual accountable for the security of every system it operates" — or tighten hint 1 to distinguish scope from specificity: "Mandatory and technology- or step-specific = standard or procedure; mandatory but stated as organisational intent that applies everywhere = policy."

findings.defect: give-away / trivial — the whole discrimination rule sits in the prompt
findings.why: The hints array is empty because the hint text was folded into the prompt, including "A code is not a memory factor just because it can be read out — what was enrolled is the device that generates it." That sentence single-handedly settles "A rotating code read from an authenticator app registered to one handset", which is the only item in the bank that requires any discrimination; the remaining five are direct keyword matches to the prompt's own gloss ("stored only in your memory", "a specific enrolled device", "a measurement of your body"). The bank measures reading, not knowledge, and the item that would have discriminated is pre-solved.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the "a code is not a memory factor" sentence back into a hint so it is revealed only on a wrong attempt, and keep the prompt to "For each sign-in step, decide which factor category it draws on."

findings.item: A vendor ignores your reports of a medical-device firmware flaw while patients remain at risk, and you keep pressing for a fix
findings.defect: redundant with a sibling item; compound stem
findings.why: This tests the same discrimination as "You report a vulnerability you found in a city's emergency dispatch system" — public-safety vulnerability disclosure → Canon I — so one of the eight slots buys no new information. It is also the only item written as a two-clause scenario (vendor behaviour + your response), which invites candidates to classify the vendor's conduct rather than their own, and introduces a counterparty (the vendor) that can be misread as a principal.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with a different Canon I subject, e.g. "You refuse to build an undocumented remote-access channel into a utility control system a customer asked you to install", and keep the medical-device scenario for the module's open-ended synthesis step.

findings.item: Where practical, prefer a passphrase of four or more words
findings.why: Hint 2 ("Anything you could decline to follow without breaking a rule is a guideline, however sensible it sounds") plus the stem's "Where practical, prefer" makes this the only non-mandatory item in the bank and hands the answer outright. It is the sole Guideline item, so the entire Guideline bucket is decided by a single lexical cue.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a second, mandatory-sounding guideline (e.g. "Security teams should consider reviewing firewall rules quarterly") so the bucket is not settled by one hedge phrase, and make hint 2 point at the test rather than the answer.

findings.item: To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
findings.why: Both Procedure items are numbered/sequenced click-paths; "Step 1: open the admin console..." already establishes the pattern, so the second adds no discrimination. A stronger Procedure item would be one that does not look like a step list on its face.
findings.suggested_fix: Swap in something that reads like prose but is still a procedure, e.g. "On termination, HR notifies IT the same day and IT disables the account before the employee leaves the building."

findings.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
findings.why: Separation of duties is an administrative/managerial control in ISC2 terms, but "on payment approvals" evokes a workflow enforced by the payment system, which some candidates will read as technical. The bank has no hints to resolve it.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword as "A rule that the person who raises a payment cannot be the person who approves it" to keep the emphasis on the rule rather than the system.

findings.defect: no hints at all; uneven bucket coverage
findings.why: The hints array is empty for a four-bucket bank, so a candidate who misreads "Discontinue the legacy file-sharing service entirely" as mitigation (removing the exposure reduces risk) gets no scaffold back to Avoid. Coverage is also 2 Mitigate / 2 Transfer / 1 Avoid / 1 Accept, so the two least-practised treatments each rest on a single item.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one hint — "Ask whether the risk still exists afterwards: reduced (mitigate), owned by someone else (transfer), gone because the activity stopped (avoid), or unchanged and knowingly signed off (accept)" — and add a second Avoid item.

findings.why: All six items are canonical textbook pairings (locked door / fence = physical, firewall / FDE = technical, background checks / AUP = administrative) with no item that could plausibly sit in two type buckets, so the gate cannot fail a candidate who has skimmed the material once. The hints add a function-vs-type warning that no item actually exercises.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one genuine two-home item that the hints then resolve, e.g. "A badge reader that logs every entry to the server room" (physical enforcement, technical logging), or an item whose function is detective to make hint 2 load-bearing.

findings.defect: two-home (integrity of the backup vs availability of the data)
findings.why: "Immutable" is an integrity word, and a candidate primed by the gate bank's integrity items may read the item as protecting the backup from alteration rather than keeping the records reachable. The prompt's "reachable through any disruption" framing makes IN the defensible answer, so this is a wobble rather than a trap.
findings.suggested_fix: If it needs hardening, "Offline backups held in a separate facility" removes the integrity cue without changing the answer.
